paper_title: OpenRUA: Robot-Use Agents Are Zero-Shot Visuomotor Policies

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Coding agents are extending their reach into the physical world by writing and executing robot control programs. One might expect the agents to use the existing mature software stack that engineers have developed over decades to access sensors and control motion. Yet prior work primarily engineers complex custom harnesses to orchestrate agents for robot use, particularly by prescribing specialized workflows and providing bespoke interfaces. This raises the question: "Is such additional harness engineering necessary?" We introduce OpenRUA, a zero-abstraction harness that bypasses bespoke abstraction layers by providing off-the-shelf coding agents with only terminal access to the robot's native software interface ROS 2. OpenRUA employs a minimalist workspace-as-harness design, only offering ROS 2 documentation and basic tools while leaving the coding agent to organize its own work without orchestrating any agentic workflow. Within this workspace, OpenRUA recasts perception as file I/O and manipulation as coding. With Claude Code powered by Claude Opus 5, OpenRUA achieves success rates of 99.0% on CaP-Bench and 87.0% on LIBERO-PRO, demonstrating that an off-the-shelf coding agent can serve as a zero-shot visuomotor policy through the robot's native interface, without bespoke primitives or task-specific training. Under this minimalist design, further analysis reveals striking emergent behaviors of coding agents: (1) For perception, the agent spontaneously writes programs that process raw sensory inputs and derive metric measurements in 96.80% of episodes. (2) For manipulation, the agent spontaneously builds motion-control clients (e.g., gripper control) in 95.87% of episodes and closed-loop control programs (e.g., adjusting motion based on sensor feedback) in 50.13% of episodes. Our code is available at https://github.com/terminalworld/OpenRUA.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Robot control has long been engineered by writing explicit programs that translate task specifications into physical motion (Fikes & Nilsson, 1971; Li et al., 1994; Siciliano et al., 2009). These programs execute on multi-layered software stack, through which human engineers coordinate drivers, messaging, planning, and actuation to implement the required behavior (Macenski et al., 2022; Garcıa et al., 2020). However, this process requires substantial effort and human expertise, with further engineering often needed for new tasks or environments. One path is to learn end-to-end visuomotor policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Team, 2025; Kim et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2026; Bjorck et al., 2025) and World Action Models (WAMs) (Agarwal et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), that map visual observations and language instructions directly to low-level actions. However, they require large-scale demonstration data, and their generalization remains limited beyond the training distribution (Zhou et al., 2025; Fei et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026). For example, LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025) reports that OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024) and π0 (Black et al., 2024), despite average success rates above 90% on standard LIBERO, achieve 0.0% success under position and task perturbations. sections.content: Figure 1: OpenRUA: minimalist workspace-as-harness for robot-use agents. Given task such as placing the block in the bowl, OpenRUA enables any off-the-shelf coding agent to operate real or simulated robot through its native ROS 2 interface, bypassing bespoke abstraction layers. The workspace serves as the harness by only providing ROS 2 documentation and basic tools, making robot perception accessible through file I/O and manipulation through coding, without orchestrating any agentic workflow. Within this workspace, the agent exhibits emergent perception and control capabilities as it works to complete the task. It writes and executes ros2cli commands or rclpy programs that send control requests to the robots controllers, here grasping and lifting the wooden block. The agent saves new RGB-D observations as workspace files and uses images, computed measurements, and terminal feedback to autonomously verify progress and refine its actions until the block is placed in the bowl. Another path is to revisit explicit programming for robot control (Fu et al., 2026), while replacing the human engineer with modern coding agents such as Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025) or Codex (OpenAI, 2025). Such an approach is known as Code as Policies (CaP) (Liang et al., 2023), where the policy itself can be inspected, edited, and debugged by the coding agent without retraining (Elmaaroufi et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). As result, the coding agent acts as Robot-Use Agent (RUA) (Isola, 2026), operating the robot the way it operates computer (Team, 2025; Fu et al., 2026; Robocurve, 2026; Berman et al., 2026). Despite this progress, existing RUA systems devote significant effort to engineering custom harnesses for robot use, especially designing the tool interfaces and primitive libraries through which agents compose policies to operate robots in prescribed workflows. These systems either wrap learned visuomotor policies as callable tools (Zhang et al., 2026b; Galanti et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a) or hand-craft custom libraries of perception and control primitives based on human expertise (Fu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). However, it remains unclear whether such additional harness engineering is necessary for coding agents to operate robots effectively, given that robots have mature ecosystem of software interfaces developed over decades for human engineers to access sensors and control motion (Macenski et al., 2022; Garcıa et al., 2020). This raises the question: Can an off-the-shelf coding agent serve as zero-shot visuomotor policy through the robots native software interface, without relying on bespoke primitives or learned policies? In this work, we introduce OpenRUA, zero-abstraction harness for robot-use agents that builds on the robots native interface, Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) (Macenski et al., 2022), the de facto standard of the robotics community. OpenRUA bypasses bespoke abstraction layers by offering off-the-shelf coding agents only terminal access to ROS 2, allowing them to operate the robot as human engineer would. As illustrated in Figure 1, OpenRUA frames robot use as live, interactive software project and employs minimalist workspace-as-harness design. This design rests on the observation that frontier coding agents already operate autonomously on unfamiliar repositories to complete tasks (OpenAI, 2024; Merrill et al., 2026; Chu et al., 2026). We hypothesize that the orchestration with bespoke interfaces in existing RUA systems compensates for limited agent capability rather than reflecting

Specifically, the workspace serves as the harness by only offering ROS 2 documentation and basic tools, leaving the coding agent to organize its own work without prescribed agentic workflow. Within this workspace, OpenRUA recasts perception as file I/O and manipulation as coding: task-specific perception and control strategies emerge as the agent acquires observations, interprets images, computes metric measurements, and writes control programs. As result, the coding agent itself serves as zero-shot visuomotor policy: it goes from raw observations to motor commands, reasoning explicitly about geometry and iteratively refining its actions from execution feedback. We conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate OpenRUA on three widely used benchmarks, i.e., CaP-Bench (Fu et al., 2026), LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025), and RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), in zero-shot setting without access to privileged simulator state and the benchmarks success predicates. With Claude Code powered by Claude Opus 5, OpenRUA achieves success rates of 99.0% on CaP-Bench and 87.0% on LIBERO-PRO, exceeding leading systems such as ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) and Harness VLA (Zhang et al., 2026b) by 18.0 and 4.6 percentage points, respectively. On unseen composite tasks in RoboCasa365, OpenRUA achieves 28.1% success, exceeding Harness VLA by 13.1 percentage points. The results show that an off-the-shelf coding agent can serve as zero-shot visuomotor policy through the robots native software interface, without bespoke primitives or learned policies. Further analysis reveals several findings about emergent agent capabilities: 1 For perception, the agent spontaneously writes programs that process raw sensory inputs (e.g., cropping images, adding grids, and reconstructing point clouds from depth) and derive metric measurements (e.g., computing coordinates for Cartesian motion targets) in 96.80% of episodes. 2 For manipulation, the agent spontaneously builds its own motion-control clients (e.g., trajectory execution and gripper control) in 95.87% of episodes and closed-loop control programs (e.g., adjusting motion or stopping based on sensor feedback) in 50.13% of episodes. 3 On RoboCasa365, OpenRUA maintains comparable success rates on seen and unseen composite tasks (26.3% and 28.1%, respectively), whereas RLDX1 drops to 5.0% and Harness VLA, which orchestrates RLDX-1, drops to 13.8% on unseen tasks. This contrast highlights the generalization potential of OpenRUA without reliance on learned robot policy. 4 Increasing test-time computation through more interaction or greater reasoning effort improves task success without additional robot training or bespoke primitives, while performance eventually saturates at levels that vary across models.

sections.title: 2 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK
sections.content: We review visuomotor policies, robot-use agents, and CLI coding agents, and introduce the Robot Operating System; an extended version is provided in Appendix A. Visuomotor Policies. visuomotor policy maps raw sensory observations directly to low-level robot actions (Levine et al., 2016). Such policies are predominantly learned end to end from robot demonstrations, as in VLA models (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Team, 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2026) and WAMs (Agarwal et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). However, their generalization remains bounded by the training distribution (Zhou et al., 2025; Fei et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026). OpenRUA instead casts an off-the-shelf coding agent as zero-shot visuomotor policy, requiring no robot demonstration data or fine-tuning. Robot-Use Agents. RUA (Isola, 2026) refers to LLM agents that operate robot the way they operate computer, through tool calls or executable programs, paradigm that traces back to CaP (Liang et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2022). One line of work wraps learned visuomotor policies as callable tools, with the agent decomposing tasks and selecting tools while the underlying policies handle physical execution (ichter et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026b; Galanti et al., 2026). Another exposes low-level actions directly to the agent, which specifies end-effector poses step by step or writes control programs using predefined, hand-crafted primitives (Hu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026). OpenRUA instead provides the coding agent with only terminal access to the robots native ROS 2 interfaces and workspace, allowing it to build task-specific perception and control tools during execution rather than requiring them to be engineered in advance. CLI Coding Agents. CLI coding agents such as Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025) and Codex (OpenAI, 2025) resolve real-world software engineering tasks through autonomous iteration (OpenAI,

These agents exhibit closed-loop agency over long horizons: they navigate codebases, edit and run code, issue CLI commands, interpret terminal output, and recover from errors. OpenRUA turns this competence toward robot control by treating the robot as live software project, allowing the agent to apply these capabilities to physical tasks without adaptation. Robot Operating System. ROS 2 connects robot components and exposes their sensing, state, and control capabilities via topics, services, and actions (Macenski et al., 2022). The native ros2cli command-line tools and rclpy Python client library allow developers to inspect these interfaces, acquire data, and send control requests. Prior work connects LLM agents to ROS through an additional abstraction layer of custom tools or predefined primitives, with evaluations limited to in-house tasks rather than standard robot control benchmarks (Royce et al., 2024; Mower et al., 2024).

sections.title: 3 OPENRUA: WORKSPACE AS HARNESS FOR ROBOT-USE AGENTS
sections.content: Given natural-language task, OpenRUA provides an off-the-shelf coding agent with only terminal access to the robots native ROS 2 interface and workspace on the robots computer (Figure 1). The zero-abstraction design exposes the robots existing ROS 2 interfaces without introducing an additional agent-specific interface layer. The workspace provides ROS 2 documentation and basic starter tools for the agent to explore the robot, and stores the observations, programs, and notes the agent produces during execution. Within this workspace, OpenRUA recasts perception as file I/O and manipulation as coding. We expect task-specific perception and control strategies to emerge as the agent explores this workspace, writes and tests programs, and uses execution feedback to refine its solutions, much as it would when working on an unfamiliar software project. Without orchestrating any agentic workflow, OpenRUA allows the agent itself to decide when to observe, which commands or programs to write and execute, and how to verify task completion. The tools are provided as source files; the agent can inspect and adapt them, use them as references, or write its own programs using the native ROS 2 interfaces. During task execution, the workspace itself also serves as an external, persistent memory, preserving observations and intermediate results beyond the agents context window. We expect the agent to autonomously organize images, programs, notes, and logs into folders such as snaps/, scripts/, and work/. By revisiting them, the agent can recover prior findings, reuse or revise earlier programs, and build on prior work as the task progresses. Perception as File I/O. OpenRUA reformulates robot perception as standard file I/O task, allowing the agent to acquire data from the robots native ROS 2 sensor topics and save it as workspace files. Depending on the robots available sensors and interfaces, these files can contain 1 visual data (e.g., RGB and depth images); 2 proprioceptive and kinematic states (e.g., joint states and frame transforms); and 3 force and effort feedback (e.g., force/torque readings and joint efforts); see Appendix B.3 for details. The agent can run the supplied starter tools, adapt their source code, or write its own rclpy programs to subscribe to the relevant topics and save the received data. The saved files are accessible through the agents built-in file tools: images can be opened for visual inspection, while numerical arrays and structured text can be read by programs for computation. The agent is left to decide when to acquire new observations, which files to inspect, and what processing code to write based on the task and execution feedback. We examine the agents perception strategies that emerge under this design in Section 4.3. Manipulation as CLI Coding. OpenRUA reformulates robot manipulation as CLI coding task, allowing the agent to write and execute ros2cli commands or rclpy programs in the terminal. These commands and programs send trajectory, velocity, or gripper control requests through native ROS 2 interfaces to the robots controllers, which execute the requests to produce physical motion. The agent is free to issue commands step by step and inspect feedback between actions, or write programs that run closed-loop control using sensor feedback. The agent can inspect terminal output and acquire new observations to assess execution outcomes and revise its commands or programs. We examine the agents control strategies that emerge under this design in Section 4.4.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate OpenRUA on three simulation benchmarks: 1 CaP-Bench (Fu et al., 2026) covers seven single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks; we follow its protocol of 100 trials per task. 2 LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025) evaluates robustness to position and task perturbations across four LIBERO suites; we run ten trials per task, following prior work (Zhang et al., 2026b;a; Galanti et al., 2026). 3 RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026) evaluates mobile manipulation on atomic and composite kitchen tasks; we use its 50 target tasks with ten trials per task, following prior work (Zhang et al., 2026b). We report success rates under each benchmarks official success predicate; task coverage, sampling, and scoring details are provided in Appendix C. Agents and Models. We evaluate OpenRUA with Claude Code powered by Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5, and Fable 5.1, all at high reasoning effort, and with Codex powered by GPT-6 Astra at medium and high reasoning effort. Each episode starts with fresh workspace, without robot demonstrations, task-specific rehearsal, or memory from earlier episodes. The agent has no access to privileged simulator state or the benchmarks success predicate (see Appendix C.2 for the evaluation protocol).

Accumulating skills over predefined primitives does not supply sensing capabilities absent from their interface, whereas native ROS 2 access allows the agent to incorporate force feedback directly into its insertion program. Detailed comparisons and analysis are provided in Appendices D.1 and D.2. We further evaluate the generalization of OpenRUA on RoboCasa365 in Section 4.5.

sections.title: Episodes
sections.content: The agent builds its own tools for metric measurement to guide physical actions. Beyond visual understanding, manipulation requires numerical measurements such as target positions, object dimensions, and contact forces. Crucially, the agent constructs its own measurement programs during task execution, combining depth arrays with camera intrinsics and frame transforms to derive task-specific measurements. We observe this emergent behavior in 96.80% of episodes across CaP-Bench and LIBERO-PRO  (Table 2)  , showing that selfwritten measurement programs are common part of its approach to manipulation. For example, in Figure 4(b), the agent writes Python program to segment the nut and pegs by height and compute their positions in world coordinates from the depth array, as shown in Figure 3. The resulting coordinates provide motion targets, while measurements such as the grippers finger gap help the agent check execution outcomes. Appendix E.3 provides further details and examples. Figure 3: An agent-written program for locating the nut and pegs from depth. See Appendix for further code details. The agent autonomously pulls observations on demand. Rather than passively receiving sensory streams that continuously fill its context window, the agent actively decides which observations to fetch and when, based on the task and execution feedback. For example, in Figure 4, the agent selectively captures (a) an overhead image to locate the nut and pegs and (d) an eye-in-hand image to verify the grasp, rather than reading every camera frame throughout execution. In this way, the agent controls what sensory information enters its context, using selected observations to verify progress and guide subsequent actions. Further details are provided in Appendix B.3.

sections.title: 4.6 SCALING WITH CODING AGENTS AND MODELS
sections.content: Figure 8 shows how success rates change with increasing test-time computation (e.g., agent turns, output tokens, reasoning effort) across coding agents and models on the LIBERO-10 suite of LIBERO-PRO; detailed interaction and cost profiles are provided in Appendix F. Test-time computation improves robot control through zero-abstraction interface. Increasing the agent-turn budget from 100 to 200 raises the success rate of Claude Code with Opus 5 from 50% to 70% (Figure 8a). Increasing reasoning effort also improves performance: Codex with GPT-6 Astra reaches 69.0% at high effort, compared with 62.5% at medium effort. Both agents use the same workspace and native interface, so these gains require no additional tools or primitives to be engineered in advance. The gains nevertheless diminish as the curves flatten, while differences between models persist: Sonnet 5 reaches 24.0% despite continuing to gain successes up to about 400 turns, compared with 72.5% for Opus 5 and 75.0% for Fable 5.1. Thus, more interaction and greater reasoning effort improve performance under our native, zero-abstraction interface, while the achievable performance remains dependent on the underlying model. Detailed comparisons of interaction patterns, costs, and per-task results are provided in Appendix F.

sections.title: 4.7 FAILURE STUDY
sections.content: We analyze the failed episodes of OpenRUA with Claude Code and Opus 5 across all three benchmarks, assigning each to the stage at which the decisive error lies. The study covers 413 failed episodes  (Table 5)  . The classifications are based on transcripts, workspace files, and benchmark predicates; the detailed procedure and classification limitations are provided in Appendix G. Task criteria and undocumented machine behavior account for many failures. Classes A, B, and account for 238 of the 413 failures (58%). The agent may complete its interpretation of an instruction while missing numerical threshold or spatial region required by the benchmark predicate. For example, in 14 drawer episodes, it pulls the drawer 62136 mm and stops, whereas the predicate requires more than 140 mm. Other episodes involve conflicting task criteria or budgets exhausted while handling undocumented machine behavior, such as mobile base displaced by contact forces or freezer door that closes while the agent fetches another tray. These cases expose gap between task instructions, machine behavior, and completion criteria in current benchmarks. Physical constraints remain challenge for agent-written programs. Class accounts for 75 failures (18%), involving gripper geometry, contact forces, and reachability. Examples include object widths near or beyond the gripper opening, thin objects squeezed out during transport, and dropped objects that the arm cannot reach. The same tasks can succeed under other initial conditions, so these cases identify limited operating margins rather than tasks that are universally impossible. The agent also makes control, perception, and execution-management errors. Class accounts for 100 failures (24%): 46 control errors, 27 perception errors, and 27 waiting errors. Control errors include an incorrect gripper-width command despite measured handle width, an inverse-kinematics branch change that sends the hand below the table, and releasing an object before the arm arrives. Perception errors include failing to search for target outside the current view, while waiting errors include spending the budget polling background jobs. Thus, the ability to write measurement and feedback programs does not ensure that the agent uses them correctly or verifies every required condition. Detailed sub-causes and case sequences are provided in Appendix G.

sections.title: 5 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Although ROS 2 is de facto standard used in both simulation and on physical robots (Macenski et al., 2022), shared software interface alone does not establish that our results generalize to realworld deployment. Our evaluation is limited to simulation; experiments on physical robots are needed to assess the practical viability of OpenRUA, particularly in three respects. Timing. We follow common simulation evaluation protocols (Fu et al., 2026; Galanti et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2024), in which simulation time advances during action execution but pauses during agent deliberation (Appendix C.2). Thus, our evaluation does not capture the effects of inference latency on physical environment that continues to evolve during deliberation. Agent-written feedback controllers can react to sensor readings within running program, but do not eliminate delays between agent-level decisions. Real-time responsiveness remains to be evaluated, especially for dynamic tasks.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Sensing. Although the agent receives raw simulated sensor data rather than privileged object states, these observations do not capture the full variability of real-world sensing. Sensor noise, missing depth values, and calibration errors may affect both visual interpretation and programmatic measurement. The agents demonstrated perception capabilities in simulation therefore do not establish robustness to real-world sensor data. Physical-robot experiments are needed to test whether agentwritten perception programs can detect and accommodate such errors. Safety. Task success does not establish safe execution: our failure analysis includes motions that would collide with the table. Although agents sometimes write their own force thresholds and stopping conditions, these protections are not guaranteed to be present or correct. Physical deployment would require independently enforced safety controls, such as motion limits, collision checks, and emergency stops, rather than relying solely on agent-written safeguards. Validating these controls while retaining the agents flexibility remains future work.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented OpenRUA, zero-abstraction harness that provides off-the-shelf coding agents with terminal access to the robots native ROS 2 interface. Its minimalist workspace-as-harness design places machine documentation and basic tools in workspace, leaving the agent to organize its own work without prescribed agentic workflow. It recasts perception as file I/O and manipulation as coding. Experiments show that coding agents can serve as zero-shot visuomotor policies without learned robot policies or task-specific primitive libraries. Crucially, image-processing tools, metric measurement programs, motion-control clients, and feedback controllers emerge as the agent writes code during execution. The findings suggest that robot-use agents need not depend on an expanding set of human-engineered abstractions; the robots existing software stack can support agents in constructing the tools they need. Our work highlights the potential for continued advances in coding agents to unlock increasingly general capabilities, extending from software tasks to interaction with the physical world.

sections.title: A EXTENDED RELATED WORK
sections.content: Visuomotor Policies. visuomotor policy maps raw sensory observations, such as camera images and proprioceptive states, directly to low-level robot actions (Levine et al., 2016). Today such policies are predominantly learned end to end: VLA models attach an action head to pretrained vision-language backbone and fine-tune it on robot demonstrations (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Team, 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2026), and WAM variants extend this line by jointly predicting future observations and actions (Agarwal et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). However, they require large-scale demonstration data, and their generalization remains bounded by the training distribution: performance drops sharply under perturbations of objects, lighting, and poses (Zhou et al., 2025; Fei et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026). OpenRUA instead casts an off-the-shelf coding agent as zero-shot visuomotor policy, requiring no robot demonstration data or fine-tuning. Robot-Use Agents. RUA (Isola, 2026) refers to LLM agents that operate robot the way they operate computer, paradigm that traces back to CaP, in which an LLM writes executable programs as robot policies (Liang et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2022). By composing predefined perception and control primitives, CaP brings the LLMs world knowledge about geometry, physics, and programming to robot control without any robot demonstrations (Kumar, 2026). Driven by frontier coding agents, todays RUA systems have extended CaP from one-shot code generation to an agentic loop: the agent acts through tool calls or generated programs, observes the outcome, and revises its next action (Team, 2025; Fu et al., 2026; Robocurve, 2026; Berman et al., 2026). These systems broadly fall into two categories based on the interface through which the agent acts. One line of work wraps learned visuomotor policies into callable tools, yielding hierarchical architecture in which the high-level LLM agent decomposes tasks and selects tools while the low-level policy handles physical execution (ichter et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026b; Galanti et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a). However, delegating low-level execution to learned policy can limit the agents ability to diagnose and correct failures in out-of-distribution scenes (Chen et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Another line of work exposes lowlevel actions directly to the agent, which itself serves as the robot policy (Jia et al., 2026; Berman et al., 2026; Robocurve, 2026; Su et al., 2026), either by issuing end-effector poses step by step (Hu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026) or by writing the control code with predefined primitives (Fu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026). Nevertheless, these systems either read privileged simulator state (e.g., ground-truth object poses) that is unavailable on real hardware (Singh et al., 2025; Tsui et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026), or rely on custom, hand-crafted library of perception and control primitives (e.g., pose estimators and grasp samplers), which requires re-engineering for each new embodiment (Fu et al., 2026; Seker et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). OpenRUA instead provides the coding agent with terminal access to the robots native ROS 2 interfaces and workspace, allowing it to construct perception and control programs during execution. ROS 2 is de facto standard used in both simulation and on physical robots (Macenski et al., 2022); our evaluation is limited to simulation, as discussed in Section 5. CLI Coding Agents. CLI coding agents, exemplified by Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025) and Codex (OpenAI, 2025), have emerged as general-purpose agents that resolve real-world software engineering tasks, as measured by benchmarks such as SWE-bench (OpenAI, 2024) and TerminalBench (Merrill et al., 2026). These agents exhibit strong closed-loop agency over long horizons: they navigate large, complex codebases, form and test hypotheses by editing and running code, issue CLI commands and interpret terminal output, and recover from their own errors through hours of autonomous iteration. Recently, this competence has extended beyond software engineering to operating desktop and web applications (Yang et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026) and driving scientific discovery workflows (Wang et al., 2026b; Terminal-Bench-Science Team, 2026). OpenRUA turns this competence toward robot control by treating the robot as live software project, in which the coding agent can transfer its strong capabilities to physical tasks without any adaptation. Robot Operating System. ROS 2 provides software framework that connects robot components and exposes their sensing, state, and control capabilities through common communication interfaces (Macenski et al., 2022). Topics carry streams such as camera images and joint states, services answer requests such as inverse kinematics queries, and actions support longer-running operations such as trajectory execution, with feedback and results. The native ros2cli command-line tools

Robot controllers then execute the motion requests, while sensor and state interfaces provide feedback about the resulting physical changes. Prior work connects LLM agents to ROS through an additional abstraction layer of custom tools or predefined action libraries, with evaluations limited to in-house tasks rather than standard robot control benchmarks (Royce et al., 2024; Mower et al., 2024).

sections.title: B HARNESS AND WORKSPACE
sections.content: B.1 NATIVE ROS INTERFACES ROS 2 organizes robot software into nodes that exchange typed messages through topics, services, and actions (Macenski et al., 2022). These communication mechanisms connect sensor drivers, state estimation, planning, and control components. The available names, message types, coordinate frames, and units depend on the robot and are described in the workspace documentation. Communication and execution. Topics support publishsubscribe communication for sensor and state streams and for commands such as Cartesian velocities. Services return response to request, for example an inverse-kinematics solution for target pose. Actions accept execution goals and provide feedback and final result, with support for cancellation; joint-trajectory execution is one example. Controllers handle motion requests through the corresponding interfaces, while sensor and state messages report the robots evolving physical state. The observation message types and file representations are detailed in Appendix B.3, and the trajectory, gripper, and velocity interfaces in Appendix B.4. Terminal and programmatic access. The ros2cli tools can list available interfaces, inspect their types, read or publish messages, call services, and send action goals. For example, ros2 topic list -t lists topics and their message types, while ros2 interface show <type> displays the fields of an interface definition. The rclpy library provides Python access to these same communication mechanisms through subscriptions, publishers, and service and action clients. program can keep these connections active and process incoming messages through callbacks, allowing sensor readings and motion updates to be combined in running feedback loop. Both entry points belong to the existing ROS 2 development tools; OpenRUA does not require an additional agent-specific API to invoke them. B.2 WORKSPACE The initial workspace contains README.md, machine.yaml, documentation, and ordinary source files for basic operations such as saving camera observations and sending motion requests. The machine description specifies the robots sensors, control interfaces, joint limits, and coordinate frames. The README directs the agent to these resources; the agent can inspect or modify starter tools and write additional programs through its existing terminal and file capabilities. The workspace does not contain task solutions or findings from previous episodes. The opening prompt is reproduced in Figure 2a; only its task placeholder changes between episodes. It asks the agent to survey the machine, carry out the task, and verify the result without prescribing sequence of perception or manipulation steps. During an episode, the agent can retain observations, numerical measurements, programs, notes, and logs in the workspace. These files persist within the episode, including across resumed session, but are not transferred to the next episode. The evaluator remains separate as described in Appendix C.2. Provided guidance. The documentation includes recommendations for acquiring and checking observations, computing coordinates, and using sensor feedback, together with generic working patterns. The starter tools include pixel back-projection and an odometry-based mobile-base controller. These resources provide initial guidance and executable examples; the agent chooses which to use, modify, or replace when developing its task-specific solution. The complete initial documents and starter-tool source are reproduced in Appendix H.

sections.content: B.3 OBSERVATION ACQUISITION AND FILE REPRESENTATIONS The agent obtains observations through the interfaces described in machine.yaml and the workspace documentation. The acquisition methods below are alternatives the agent can select or combine according to its needs, rather than prescribed sequence. Available data and interface discovery. RGB and depth topics use sensor msgs/msg/ Image messages. Camera intrinsics are provided in sensor msgs/msg/CameraInfo messages. Joint-state messages use sensor msgs/msg/JointState and associate joint names with positions, velocities, and available efforts. Some robots also expose wrist force and torque as geometry msgs/msg/WrenchStamped messages and base odometry as nav msgs/msg/ Odometry messages. The machine description identifies the available sensors and ports; these modalities are not assumed to be present on every robot. The agent can inspect the running graph with ros2 topic list, examine topic with ros2 topic info, and inspect its message definition with ros2 interface show. Small messages, such as joint states or camera intrinsics, can be read through ros2 topic echo <topic> --once, with the output optionally redirected to workspace file. Image and numerical files. The starter tool tools/perception/cam snap.py subscribes to an image topic and saves one received frame. It accepts either camera name or full topic path and an optional output filename. For color image, it converts the ROS message with cv bridge and writes PNG. For depth image, it preserves the numerical array in .npy file and writes separate PNG visualization. The visualization rescales depth values for display; metric calculations use the original array and its documented units. The agent can inspect or modify this tool, or write an rclpy subscriber to save selected message fields in format suited to subsequent processing. For joint data, values must remain associated with their joint names rather than be interpreted using an assumed message order. Calibration, coordinate frames, and timing. Geometric calculations require the camera intrinsics and the relation between the camera frame and the desired reference frame. The agent can retrieve intrinsics from CameraInfo and query available frame transforms through tf2; the workspace documentation describes machine-specific alternatives when the required transform is unavailable. Saving RGB and depth separately does not itself guarantee temporal alignment: the starter snapshot tool captures single topic and does not synchronize multiple streams. When computation requires aligned observations, an agent-written acquisition program must account for message timestamps and the correspondence between image pixels, calibration, and coordinate frames. This is particularly relevant when either the robot or the observed scene moves between captures. sections.title: C EVALUATION PROTOCOL AND COMPARED SYSTEMS
sections.content: C.1 BENCHMARKS AND TRIAL SAMPLING The main evaluation contains 2,000 episodes: 700 on CaP-Bench, 800 on LIBERO-PRO, and 500 on RoboCasa365. All three benchmarks are evaluated in simulation using their task definitions and success predicates. CaP-Bench. We evaluate Lift, Stack, Wipe, Nut, Restack, Two-Arm Lift, and Handover, with 100 trials per task (Fu et al., 2026). The last two tasks use two Panda arms; the others use one. Trial identifiers range from 1 to 100, following the benchmarks evaluation grid. The benchmarks reset implementation samples object placements randomly; these identifiers do not specify fixed set of reproducible initial placements. Our trial count therefore matches the published protocol, but the initial states are not paired episode by episode with those of prior systems. LIBERO-PRO. We evaluate the Object, Spatial, Goal, and LIBERO-10 suites under two perturbations: initial-position swaps (P in Table 1) and task-instruction changes (T) (Zhou et al., 2025). Each of the eight suiteperturbation cells contains ten tasks, and we use initial-state indices 09 from the released initial-state files for each task. This gives 100 trials per cell and 800 trials overall. The six Object, Spatial, and Goal cells form the 600-episode subset shared with several prior codingagent evaluations; the two LIBERO-10 cells add 200 episodes. We retain the benchmarks perturbed scenes and task instructions and do not select initial states based on OpenRUA performance. The ten-trial count follows recent agent evaluations (Zhang et al., 2026b;a; Galanti et al., 2026); some earlier systems instead report 50 trials per task, as described in Appendix C.4. RoboCasa365. We use the target50 evaluation set in the benchmarks target kitchen split: 18 Atomic-Seen tasks, 16 Composite-Seen tasks, and 16 Composite-Unseen tasks (Nasiriany et al., 2026). Seen and Unseen refer to whether the task templates occur in the benchmarks pretraining demonstrations, rather than whether OpenRUA has previously attempted them. Every task is evaluated for ten trials, using seeds 09, for 180, 160, and 160 episodes in the three groups. Each reset uses the benchmarks sampler to select an allowed kitchen layout and style, object instances, and placements; we do not force one trial per kitchen. Harness VLA uses the same task groups but evaluates ten held-out seeds per atomic task and five per composite task after separate reference-seed exploration (Zhang et al., 2026b). Our ten-trial setting thus follows its atomic-task evaluation count and applies that count to all three groups, without reference-seed exploration. The GR00T results reproduced from the RoboCasa365 paper use 30 trials per task, as specified in its Appendix G.2. C.2 AGENT CONFIGURATION AND EXECUTION PROTOCOL The main experiments use Claude Code with Claude Opus 5 and high reasoning effort. Each episode uses the same workspace template for its robot configuration and fresh agent session; files and taskspecific findings are not carried between episodes. The agent receives the task instruction and the opening prompt shown in Figure 2a, with machine documentation and starter tools as described in Appendix B.2. No robot demonstrations or benchmark-specific rehearsal episodes are provided. The alternative agent and model configurations used in the scaling analysis are described in Appendix F. Simulation and control. Simulation advances when control commands trigger environment steps and remains paused between those steps, including while the agent reasons or reads observations. running control program can continue to issue commands and advance the simulation. Thus, model inference latency does not itself advance physical time. The robot exposes sensor, state, trajectory, gripper, and available velocity interfaces through ROS 2; the bridge executes these requests using the simulators robot controllers. The runs use joint-position control for arm trajectories and image observations rendered at 640 480 pixels. These execution settings differ from evaluations that feed low-resolution images to learned policy and use its operational-space action representation; the benchmark scenes and success predicates remain those of the original tasks.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Budgets and termination. An episode ends when the agent finishes, reaches 500 agent turns, or exhausts 240 minutes of active wall-clock time, whichever occurs first. There is no additional simulation-step horizon in these runs. Active wall-clock time includes reasoning and tool execution but excludes periods when an episode is suspended because model access is unavailable. Resuming suspended episode preserves its state and consumes the remaining budget rather than starting new episode. These budgets are not assumed to match those of every baseline; comparisons use the published settings of each system. Evaluation isolation. The agent runs in separate sandbox with access to the robots ROS 2 interfaces and its own workspace. The simulator implementation, privileged task-object poses, benchmark goal predicates, and evaluation records are not exposed in that workspace or as agent-callable tools. The evaluator checks success independently, and its verdict is neither returned to the agent nor used to terminate an episode early. The agent must decide when to finish using observations and execution feedback. C.3 SCORING AND AGGREGATION The evaluator checks the benchmarks original success predicate at every simulation step. An episode counts as successful if the predicate is satisfied at any step before termination; once recorded, success is retained even if the final state later changes. The agents own declaration of completion is not used as the success label. The first successful step and its timestamps are recorded for the budget analyses in Section 4.6. Success rate is the fraction of evaluated episodes that satisfy this rule. CaP-Bench averages over seven equally sized task groups. For LIBERO-PRO, Table 1 reports both the six-cell average over Object, Spatial, and Goal and the eight-cell average that also includes LIBERO-10. The latter corresponds to all 800 episodes; missing baseline cells are not imputed. For RoboCasa365, the overall rate averages over all 50 tasks, weighting Atomic-Seen, Composite-Seen, and Composite-Unseen by their task counts of 18, 16, and 16. Each main configuration is evaluated once over its stated episode set; we do not interpret small numerical differences as evidence of statistical significance. C.4 COMPARED SYSTEMS C.4.1 SOURCES AND COMPARISON SCOPE All baseline results in Tables 1 and 4 are reproduced from the cited papers or their accompanying leaderboards; we do not rerun these systems. The comparisons therefore concern published system configurations, which can differ in model, reasoning budget, available tools, prior task experience, and evaluation protocol. They are not controlled ablations that isolate the effect of the interface alone. Models and reasoning-effort settings are listed alongside the results in the main tables. Human-written programs. The CaP-Bench human reference row uses the S4 task-success values in Figure 17 of CaP-X (Fu et al., 2026): 93, 73, 100, 80, 47, 94, and 91 percent for Lift, Stack, Wipe, Nut, Restack, Two-Arm Lift, and Handover. Their arithmetic mean is 82.6%. This row represents the benchmarks expert-written programs under its low-level primitive interface, rather than new human evaluation conducted for this paper. Learned visuomotor policies. The OpenVLA, π0, and π0.5 results on the six LIBERO-PRO cells are reproduced from the comparison in CaP-X Table 2 (Fu et al., 2026). We leave the two LIBERO10 cells unreported for these rows instead of combining results from different evaluation source. The two GR00T N1.5 rows use the pretraining-only and pretraining-plus-full-target-data configurations in Table 2 of RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026). The latter includes demonstrations of the target Composite-Unseen tasks; the split name describes their absence from pretraining, not their absence from this post-training stage. We do not use the results from that papers Table 1, which evaluates different kitchen split. The RLDX-1 row is the direct frozen-policy baseline reported in Harness VLA Table 4 (Zhang et al., 2026b). Agents that orchestrate learned policies. Pigeys six-cell LIBERO-PRO row comes from its Table 2, using frozen π0.5 backend and ten trials per task (Galanti et al., 2026). Its reported zero-shot

It develops skill library before evaluation; on CaP-Bench it uses seeds 101 125 for development and evaluates generated programs on seeds 1100. C.4.2 TRAINING, EXPERIENCE, AND ORACLE ACCESS The table annotations distinguish three aspects of each reported configuration. Training indicates whether robot policy is trained on demonstrations. Experience records additional preparation on the evaluation tasks or their underlying environments before the reported test episodes, such as rehearsed programs, accumulated skills, task-specific memory, or target-task adaptation. Oracle indicates whether the benchmarks success predicate is accessible during execution; access to rewards during an earlier development phase is separate issue. These annotations describe the reported configurations and are not mutually exclusive. For OpenRUA, task-specific programs and notes are produced only within the current episode and are not prior experience under this definition. Trial counts, initial states, stopping rules, and models differ across sources. For example, RHO reports 50 initial states per task on the six LIBERO-PRO cells, whereas our evaluation uses ten. Pigey scores simulation trials using the LIBERO predicate and its own completion protocol, including failure when the agent times out without declaring completion (Galanti et al., 2026); our scoring rule is specified in Appendix C.3. Accordingly, we retain source-specific evaluation settings rather than claim that every baseline shares our execution budget or termination rule.

sections.title: D ADDITIONAL COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS
sections.content: D.1 DETAILED ANALYSIS OF MAIN RESULTS The LIBERO-PRO percentages in this subsection refer to the six Object, Spatial, and Goal perturbation conditions. Robot-use agents are zero-shot visuomotor policies. OpenRUA achieves 99.0% on CaP-Bench and 91.8% on the six LIBERO-PRO conditions considered here, without learned robot policy, taskspecific primitive library, or prior task experience. For comparison, the expert-written programs achieve 82.6% on CaP-Bench and provide separate solution for each task. The demonstrationtrained policies OpenVLA, π0, and π0.5 remain at or below 12.8% on the six LIBERO-PRO conditions after scene perturbations. Among agents that construct the policy, CaP-X reaches 18.2% on these LIBERO-PRO conditions using its provided primitives. RHO, ASPIRE, and RATS reach 43.871.7% after accumulating policy repositories or skills over the provided primitives before evaluation (Elmaaroufi et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). These systems show how prior program development can improve robot use; OpenRUA constructs its programs within the current episode through native ROS 2 interfaces.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Among agents that orchestrate learned policies, Pigey combines an LLM agent with frozen π0.5 and reaches 53.3%. Harness VLA combines coding agent with learned policy and reaches 87.7%, with task-specific memory from reference-seed exploration and access to the success predicate during execution. The corresponding OpenRUA rate is 91.8% without these resources. Together, these comparisons support the main finding that the coding agent itself can serve as zero-shot visuomotor policy. The differences characterize the reported systems; their models and evaluation settings also differ, as described in Appendix C.4. D.2 NATIVE INTERFACES AND THE LIMITS OF ACCUMULATED SKILLS Experience improves performance but leaves difficult tasks unresolved. The low Nut success rates are not results from agents without prior skill development. CaP-Agent0 uses nine synthesized utilities distilled from successful CaP-Bench rollouts (Fu et al., 2026, Section 4 and Appendix H.1). RHO evolves multi-file policy repositories through repeated execution and reflective optimization (Elmaaroufi et al., 2026, Section 3), while ASPIRE accumulates validated repairs in skill library and searches over candidate programs (Lu et al., 2026, Section 2). Despite this experience accumulation, their reported Nut success rates are 0%, 1%, and 9%, respectively, compared with 100% for OpenRUA. On the LIBERO-PRO Spatial suite, the corresponding position/- task results are 12%/14% for CaP-X, 53.0%/61.6% for RHO, and 51%/60% for ASPIRE, versus 98%/100% for OpenRUA. Experience improves many tasks, but the reported optimization and skill accumulation do not close these gaps. The primitive interface constrains what experience can encode. ASPIRE explicitly identifies this limitation: programs remain bounded by the provided perception, planning, and control API; capabilities outside that API require inefficient approximation or human extension of the interface (Lu et al., 2026, Section 5). Accumulating strategies over an interface does not by itself expose an unavailable sensor or control operation. CaP-Xs documented S3/S4 simulation interface provides image observations, segmentation, grasp proposals, inverse kinematics, and joint and gripper moves, but does not list force-reading or force-conditioned motion primitive (Fu et al., 2026, Appendix G). This restriction concerns the evaluated simulation interface; CaP-X separately describes force-wrench access for its real-robot setup. CaP-X also reports difficulties with insertion requiring continuous feedback, and attributes LIBERO-PRO failures to perception errors, angled grasp proposals, and the lack of collision-aware motion planning (Fu et al., 2026, Appendices and J). Thus, the comparison concerns the capabilities available for programs to use as well as the experience accumulated in composing them. Native sensor interfaces support agent-written feedback programs. OpenRUA exposes sensor and control interfaces through ROS 2, allowing the agent to write programs that monitor physical feedback during execution. The Nut example in Figure 12(c) executes insertion in seven trajectory segments with force reading after each; Section 4.4 reports the broader use of agent-written feedback programs and motion clients. This provides concrete mechanism for using sensing during manipulation without pre-specified task primitive or learned robot policy. Harness VLA takes different route, composing analytic primitives with frozen VLA for contact-rich execution; its strongest Spatial result in Table 1 is 94% (Zhang et al., 2026b). The consequences of relying on learned policy under distribution shift are examined in Section 4.5. D.3 GENERALIZATION AND DEMONSTRATION COVERAGE This appendix expands the RoboCasa365 results in Section 4.5, examining demonstration coverage and composite-task difficulty. Target-task demonstrations improve the evaluated learned policy. The two GR00T N1.5 rows in Table 4 distinguish pretraining alone from pretraining followed by post-training on the target-task demonstrations (Nasiriany et al., 2026, Table 2). On the same 16 Composite-Unseen tasks, success rises from 0.2% to 42.1% after post-training on their demonstrations. This contrast shows the importance of demonstration coverage for the evaluated learned policy. The term Unseen refers to task templates absent from the benchmarks pretraining set; these templates are included in the target data used by the post-trained GR00T configuration. Its 42.1% therefore represents performance with target-task demonstration training, whereas the 28.1% of OpenRUA is obtained without such training.

sections.content: Harness VLA improves on RLDX-1 but retains SeenUnseen performance gap. RLDX-1 achieves 21.3% on Composite-Seen tasks and 5.0% on Composite-Unseen tasks in the frozen-policy evaluation reported by Harness VLA (Zhang et al., 2026b, Table 4). Harness VLA uses this same policy as its contact-rich execution primitive, together with analytic primitives, coding agent, taskspecific and global memory, and access to the benchmarks success predicate. With Codex, it reaches 61.0% on Seen tasks and 13.8% on Unseen tasks; with Claude Code, the corresponding rates are 47.5% and 15.0%. Both configurations improve on the underlying policy, including on Unseen tasks, but retain pronounced SeenUnseen performance gap. The comparison therefore shows that adding agent-level planning, memory, and verification does not remove this gap in the evaluated configurations: contact-rich execution still relies on the frozen robot policy. In OpenRUA, the coding agent instead constructs the control program during the episode, using current observations and the robots native sensing and control interfaces. The same workflow yields 26.3% on Seen and 28.1% on Unseen composite tasks, without learned robot policy or task-specific rehearsal. Composite tasks remain difficult despite stable SeenUnseen performance. Stable performance across Seen and Unseen templates does not imply that composite tasks are easy. The success rate of OpenRUA falls from 61.1% on Atomic-Seen tasks to 26.3% and 28.1% on the two composite groups; every compared system also performs worse on composite tasks than on atomic tasks. This atomic-to-composite comparison concerns the additional demands of composing and executing multiple steps, whereas the SeenUnseen comparison concerns task-template coverage within the composite category. Appendix examines the remaining difficulties, including incomplete longhorizon execution, physical constraints, mismatches between instructions and scoring criteria, and agent errors. Thus, the generalization result is that the absence of task template from robot pretraining data is not accompanied by lower success for OpenRUA in this evaluation, even though composite manipulation remains challenging.

sections.content: Runs behind Table 11. All runs use the same harness, workspace, and prompt on the two LIBERO-10 perturbation cells (10 tasks 10 initial states each). Claude Code with Opus 5 and Fable 5.1 ran the full 200 episodes once at high reasoning effort, Claude Codes default. Claude Code with Sonnet 5 ran the full 200 episodes at high effort. Codex with GPT-6 Astra ran the full 200 episodes twice, once at medium reasoning effort and once at high; the two runs are reported as two rows. The turn and cost profiles use the episodes with tool-call timestamps: all 200 for GPT-6 Astra at high effort, 192 for medium (the first eight episodes of that run were made before rollout logging was enabled). More interaction and greater reasoning effort improve success under the same native interface. The curves in Figure 8 are computed retrospectively from the first successful step of each recorded episode: an episode contributes to the success rate at given budget if success occurred within that budget. The agent-turn and output-token curves therefore describe when the recorded runs succeed, rather than separate runs in which the agent is instructed to work under each plotted budget. For Opus 5, the share solved within 100, 150, and 200 turns is 50%, 66%, and 70%, respectively; for Fable 5.1, it is 61%, 71%, and 72%. The reasoning-effort comparison uses separate 200-episode runs with the same Codex agent and GPT-6 Astra model: increasing effort from medium to high raises success from 62.5% to 69.0%. These improvements occur without changing the initial workspace, adding task-specific primitives, or training robot policy. The output-token curves provide complementary view of the computation consumed before success; the estimation of Claude Code token positions is described below. Performance gains diminish while differences between models persist. The Opus 5 and Fable 5.1 curves flatten within about 300 turns, whereas Sonnet 5 continues to gain successes up to about 400 turns and finishes at 24.0%. Within 100 turns, Fable 5.1 solves 61% of episodes, Opus 5 solves 50%, and Sonnet 5 solves 1%. These differences show that models vary both in final success and in the interaction needed to reach it. Failed Claude Code episodes are longer than successful ones: median turns are 131 versus 97 for Opus 5, 84 versus 72 for Fable 5.1, and 334 versus 219 for Sonnet 5. For Sonnet 5, 22% of episodes reach the 500-turn limit, and none of those episodes succeeds. Together, the curves and episode lengths show diminishing returns within the evaluated budgets, with substantial differences remaining between models. sections.title: G FAILURE STUDY
sections.content: This appendix expands the failure study in Section 4.7, including the classification procedure, detailed examples, and sub-causes. We analyzed 413 failed episodes of OpenRUA with Opus 5 from the evaluations in Tables 1 and 4, and assigned each to the stage at which its decisive error lies (Table 5; the procedure and the class definitions are given below, and Table 12 lists the sub-causes). G.1 CLASSIFICATION PROCEDURE AND SCOPE Procedure. The study analyzes 413 failed episodes of OpenRUA with Claude Code and Opus 5 in the main runs: 104 on LIBERO-PRO, 7 on CaP-Bench and 302 on RoboCasa365. For each episode we read the transcript and the agents workspace, recovered the benchmark predicate (the BDDL goal and region definitions on LIBERO, the task classs success check on RoboCasa365, the stated condition on CaP-Bench), and compared the end state the agent measured with that predicate; for RoboCasa365 the scene was re-instantiated from the episode seed to recover quantities the predicate uses but the agent cannot observe, such as region boxes and target poses. To see what the demonstrations teach, we replayed the final state of each of the 50 LIBERO demonstrations for three of the tasks in the benchmark environment: the middle drawer ends at 127 to 160 mm of travel (median 156, the joints limit is 160), the plate ends within 4 cm of the centre of the stove-front region in 49 of 50, and the bottles base rests in the racks 22 mm band in the 25 demonstrations whose final state satisfies the predicate. Each episode receives one class, the stage at which the decisive error lies, and record of whether its last message announces completion. Classes. A: the agent completed and verified its own reading of the instruction, and the predicate needs quantity or region the instruction does not state. B: the predicate contradicts the instruction (it scores another object, or region the named object cannot occupy). C: the budget is exhausted while the agent handles undocumented machine behavior, with the task still in progress and no other decisive error identified (a base without brake, doors that close themselves, fixtures whose scored joint is not the one that moves). D: the object or the required force lies at or beyond the limits of the gripper, the base or the arms reach. E: an error of the agent itself, in perception (a target never searched for, misread joint), in control (a wrong gripper width, release before arrival, trajectory through an obstacle), or in waiting (budget spent polling background jobs). Table 12 lists the sub-causes. Limits. The study reads one models episodes; the other models in Table 11 were not classified. Classes were assigned by reading and are recorded with confidence level; five LIBERO-PRO episodes (a bottle-in-drawer task) could not be resolved between class and residual drawer opening below the point-cloud resolution and are counted under A. G.2 DETAILED FINDINGS Task criteria and undocumented machine behavior account for many failures. Classes A, B, and account for 238 of the 413 analyzed failures (58%), as in Section 4.7. In class A, the agent completes and verifies its interpretation of the instruction, but the predicate requires an unstated threshold or spatial region. For example, in 14 drawer episodes it pulls 62136 mm and stops before bottle in the drawers path, while the predicate requires more than 140 mm. In seven wine-rack episodes, it places the bottle along the slope to prevent rolling, but the predicate checks its base In nine board-scrubbing episodes, against 22 mm band at the foot of the rack (Figure 19(a)). measured contact spans 310 cm, while the predicate requires 10 cm sweep. Class covers 19 episodes in which the predicate conflicts with the instruction, including goal that scores the pot initialized on the opposite side and 55 mm target slot for 100 mm mug. Class covers budgets exhausted while handling undocumented machine behavior. Examples include an unbraked base displaced by 0.150.39 during contact, freezer doors that close while the robot fetches another tray (Figure 19(b)), and faucet with two hinges of which only one is scored. The agent discovers these behaviors during execution and spends its budget writing position-holding code or repeating earlier actions.

Class accounts for 75 failures (18%), involving gripper geometry, contact forces, and reachability. The twelve LIBEROPRO cases include 106 mm bowl and 103 mm mug rims against 7280 mm gripper opening, as well as plate rims squeezed out during lifting. The same tasks succeed under other initial conditions, indicating limited operating margins rather than tasks that are universally impossible. On RoboCasa365, 63 failures involve physical constraints of the gripper, base, or arm. For example, the binary gripper can continue closing on soft or thin object during transport; the finger gap on straw decreases from 14 to 1 mm over one base drive. Contact forces above the bases 250 friction displace the robot and can raise its torso by up to 0.34 m. An object dropped onto the floor cannot be retrieved when it lies below the arms reachable height of approximately = 0.3 m. The agent also makes control, perception, and execution-management errors. Class accounts for 100 failures (24%): 46 control errors, 27 perception errors, and 27 waiting errors. Control errors include commanding 0.008 per finger on measured 0.030 handle, despite the documentations warning, and ejecting the hammer when the other arm releases it (Figure 19(c)). Other cases involve an inverse-kinematics branch change that drives the hand below the table, releasing before arrival, or knocking over an already placed object during recovery. Many RoboCasa365 cases involve target outside the current view that the agent never searches for, or an unobserved joint such as the scored hinge of faucet. The 27 waiting errors involve budget spent polling background jobs or episodes ending while monitor remains armed. Thus, the ability to write measurement and feedback programs does not ensure that the agent uses them correctly or verifies every required condition. By benchmark. Cartesian servo (kind cartesian_twist) - **What**: stream end-effector velocities for small precise motion. - **Port**: machine.yaml actuators[kind=cartesian_twist]; topic, and the frame to stamp commands with (linear is m/s). - **CLI**: ros2 topic pub --rate 20 <port> geometry_msgs/msg/TwistStamped "{header: {frame_id: <frame>}, twist: {linear: {z: -0.05}}}"; Ctrl-C to stop the stream. - **rclpy** (the world only advances while commands stream; publish in loop, then re-check sensors): python import rclpy, yaml from geometry_msgs.msg import TwistStamped tw = next(a for in yaml.safe_load(open("machine.yaml"))["actuators"] if a["kind"] == "cartesian_twist") rclpy.init(); node = rclpy.create_node("nudge") pub = node.create_publisher(TwistStamped, tw["port"], 10) msg = TwistStamped(); msg.header.frame_id = tw["frame"] msg.twist.linear.z = -0.05 for _ in range(20): # 5 cm/s downward # 1 of motion pub.publish(msg); rclpy.spin_once(node, timeout_sec=0.05) - **Notes**: burst sense correct beats one long blind stream. ## C. Gripper (kind gripper) - **What**: open/close the fingers. The manifest entry carries this grippers facts (open_m, closed_m, stops_at, max_effort), each with its definition written on the line. - **Port**: machine.yaml actuators[kind=gripper] (control_msgs/action/GripperCommand). - **Tool**: python3 tools/action/gripper_cmd.py <width_m> - **CLI** (fill <port>, open_m/closed_m, max_effort from the manifest entry): ros2 action send_goal <port> control_msgs/action/GripperCommand "{command: {position: <m>, max_effort: <n>}}" - **Notes**: after closing on something, finger positions in the joint state stop above closed_m; that gap is your grasp evidence. ## D. Mobile base (kind base_twist (only on mobile machines)) - **What**: drive the base with body-frame velocities. Absent from the manifest = this machines base is fixed; skip this section. - **Port**: machine.yaml actuators[kind=base_twist]; plain geometry_msgs/msg/Twist (/cmd_vel convention): linear.x forward, linear.y left (holonomic bases only; check type), angular.z counter-clockwise yaw. - **Tool**: python3 tools/action/base_goto.py <x> <y> [yaw]; closed-loop on odometry; exits with the last pose as fact on stall. - **CLI**: ros2 topic pub --rate 10 <port> geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.3}}"; Ctrl-C to stop. - **Semantics**: **one message = one control tick** of motion at that velocity. Messages queue up to small depth (4); anything beyond is dropped, so flooding buys nothing. Queued ticks still execute after you stop publishing; pace yourself by odometry feedback, not by message count or wall time. - **Notes**: - closed-loop is the only reliable pattern: publish few ticks read odometry (20-perception A4) correct repeat; - drive and arm motion are separate commands; position the base first, then work the arm; - operational norm for go-to/docking jobs: park the base directly in front of the target, within arms reach (close enough to work on it without re-driving), squarely facing it. "Near" is not parked. ## E. Planning (MoveIt): machine.yaml planning - **What**: collision-aware planning and IK when raw trajectories are not enough (present when planning.moveit is true). - **Ports**: planning.move_action (plan+execute, moveit_msgs/action/MoveGroup, group planning.group); planning.ik_service (moveit_msgs/srv/GetPositionIK); Cartesian pose joint positions. - **Tool**: python3 tools/action/ik_move.py <x> <y> <z> <qx> <qy> <qz> <qw> [seconds] [--at tcp]; IK then trajectory, loud on failure. - **Pattern**: IK for the target pose, then (trajectory) to go there; or move_action end-to-end when obstacles matter. - **Notes**: check the returned error_code (1 = success); frame behavior is NOT what headers suggest; see "Planning facts" below.

sections.content: ## Actuation facts - Gripper commands are PER-FINGER positions: the opening between the fingers is twice the commanded value (nominals in machine.yaml). What this machine does with the commanded value is its own fact, not general rule: read stops_at on the manifests gripper entry. Gap readings need few settle ticks; the measured maximum opening can sit slightly under nominal. - trajectory tolerance-violation result on long goal is often controller lag, not an obstruction: resending the same goal typically converges. - Arm contact and reaction forces can displace the mobile base by centimeters; re-read odometry after arm work before trusting stored base poses. ## Planning facts (MoveIt) - The planners model frame is the ARM BASE even where message headers say "world" (machine.yaml planning.planning_frame). Leave frame_id EMPTY in IK requests; base-frame label is rejected (-21). - The planning scene starts EMPTY; no world collision objects exist until you publish them; collision meshes carry roughly centimeter of padding, so trust measurements over nominals. - IK/FK requests HANG if their robot_state carries non-arm joints (finger joints included): seed with the arm joints only. - IK can fail silently (no error, no motion) and non-monotonically (nearby poses flip feasibility). Seed requests with the current configuration to keep branch continuity, and verify motion actually happened from /joint_states. Listing 5: docs/40-patterns.md # 40. Working patterns Cross-cutting habits that save turns and time. ## P1. Act verify, every time The clock only moves with activity (10-machine.md 4), so verification is sensor re-reads, never waits: 1. command (30-action) 2. re-read the relevant sensor (20-perception) 3. compare with what you intended 4. correct or continue. Motion: compare the joint state against your target. Manipulation: finger gap + fresh camera frame. World changes: before/after frames from the same camera. ## P2. Coarse-to-fine motion Large repositioning with one trajectory move (fast, accurate over big spans), final approach with short servo bursts (small, sensed, correctable). Avoid many small trajectory hops and long blind servo streams alike. ## P3. Approachgraspverify (generic pick pattern) 1. Snapshot cameras; locate the target object in the image (pixels + depth + intrinsics world position, 20-perception B3). 2. Move above it (IK trajectory), open the gripper. 3. Descend with short servo bursts, watching wrist camera if present. 4. Close the gripper; verify the grasp: finger gap above closed_m, wrench change on contact. 5. Lift and confirm visually (fresh frame) before moving on. Placing is the mirror: position above the destination, descend, open, retreat, verify with fresh frame. ## P4. Troubleshooting table Symptom Likely cause Fix --------- trajectory result error_code != 0 duration too short / target beyond joint limit slow down; check limits (machine.yaml) arm lags the servo stream per-message motion is tiny keep streaming in loop; verify between bursts gripper "closed" but nothing held closed on air reopen, re-approach lower/centered, use the wrist camera image looks stale pulled an old frame snapshot again after the motion completed
